items.title: F-35C Begins Operational Testing Aboard Ford-Class Carrier John F. Kennedy
items.originalTitle: F-35C Begins Operational Testing Aboard Ford-Class Carrier John F. Kennedy
items.summary: The United States Navy has reached a significant milestone regarding the integration of the F-35C carrier-based variant of the Joint Strike Fighter on the Ford-class nuclear powered aircraft carriers. Beginning on October 13, F-35C “Lightning II” assigned to the “Salty Dogs” Air Test and Evaluation Squadron (VX) 23 based at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, embarked on PCU John F Kennedy (CVN-79) for aircraft launch and recovery operations.

evidenceRecords.text: The United States Navy has reached a significant milestone regarding the integration of the F-35C carrier-based variant of the Joint Strike Fighter on the Ford-class nuclear powered aircraft carriers.

Beginning on October 13, F-35C “Lightning II” assigned to the “Salty Dogs” Air Test and Evaluation Squadron (VX) 23 based at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, embarked on PCU John F Kennedy (CVN-79) for aircraft launch and recovery operations.
The US Navy released several sets of imagery detailing the arrival and operation of at least two F-35C, tail numbers 401 and 403 on the yet to be commissioned aircraft carrier.
The aircraft completed arrested recovery and catapult launches from CVN-79, utilising the carrier’s distinct EMALS and AAG electromagnetic launch and recovery systems.
Protracted integration of F-35C with newest US Navy carriers The first of class USS Gerald R.
However, to date the carrier does not embark F-35C, instead exclusively relying on air wings equipped with F/A-18E/F and G-variants for combat capability.
In contrast, US Navy F-35C have been operational on older Nimitz- class carriers for six years.
The first Nimitz -class carrier to operationally deploy the fighter jet was USS Carl Vinson in 2020, after initial testing with F-35C commencing on the carrier in 2017 .
A U.S. Navy F-35C Lightning II, attached to the “Salty Dogs” of Air Test and Evaluation Squadron (VX) 23, makes an arrested landing on the flight deck aboard PCU John F.
Kennedy (CVN 79), marking the first time an F-35C lands on a Ford-class aircraft carrier.

The principal reason for the delayed induction of F-35C with Ford -class carriers is the USN decision to extend various testing and integration measures on the new carrier-design as cost-saving measure, deriving from a Congress-mandated cost cap on the CVN-78-program.

In response the House Armed Services seapower and projection forces subcommittee in its FY2020 submission included language mandating that USN must not accept CVN-79 without the ability to embark the F-35C .

items.originalTitle: Honeywell Aerospace’s counter-drone software unites data from multiple sensors into one
items.summary: Counter-drone systems can combine radar, cameras, radio-frequency sensors and other equipment to detect, track and identify potential threats. Honeywell Aerospace’s SAMURAI system is designed to bring information from those disparate sources into a single interface. The system uses UNITAS, Honeywell Aerospace’s battle-management software, to integrate sensors and effectors from different manufacturers. “There is no one solution that solves every threat out there,” said retired Air Force Col. Tom Konicki, director of business at Honeywell Aerospace.

evidenceRecords.text: The system uses UNITAS , Honeywell Aerospace’s battle-management software, to integrate sensors and effectors from different manufacturers.
Tom Konicki, director of business at Honeywell Aerospace.
Konicki said counter-drone systems need to detect, track, identify, classify and ultimately defeat drones, regardless of the operator’s intent.

“There could be seven different sensors that have identified it and are feeding that into our software.” Konicki said the interface is designed to be straightforward for operators, including younger service members who may be assigned counter-drone duties without extensive experience operating the different systems.
He said Honeywell Aerospace has demonstrated the software to U.S. government and military representatives, as well as local law enforcement and state and city representatives.
The software also uses an open-architecture approach, allowing customers to integrate equipment they already own instead of replacing it with products from a single manufacturer.
Separately, Honeywell Aerospace announced Oct. 12 that its wholly owned subsidiary, EMS Defense Technologies, was selected for a Department of Homeland Security counter-drone contract vehicle .

Konicki said Honeywell Aerospace works with international partners, including Lithuania, Slovakia and Colombia, and can integrate locally sourced equipment when customers want to use particular sensors or effectors.

items.title: Thales Australia tackles heavy battlefield logistics with new big-rig robot
items.originalTitle: Thales Australia tackles heavy battlefield logistics with new big-rig robot
items.summary: Thales Australia says it has built just such a robot. The company unveiled its BladeHaul extra-large, heavy-duty UGV on Oct. 6, the opening day of the Land Forces 2026 exhibition being held in Perth, Western Australia. Looking something akin to an aircraft tug, the BladeHaul relies on the chassis and driveline of Thales Australia’s popular Bushmaster 4x4 protected mobility vehicle that is in widespread Australian Army use.

evidenceRecords.text: Thales Australia says it has built just such a robot.
The company unveiled its BladeHaul extra-large, heavy-duty UGV on Oct. 6, the opening day of the Land Forces 2026 exhibition being held in Perth, Western Australia.

Looking something akin to an aircraft tug, the BladeHaul relies on the chassis and driveline of Thales Australia’s popular Bushmaster 4x4 protected mobility vehicle that is in widespread Australian Army use.

According to its designer, this uncrewed vehicle “is engineered to outperform all existing and planned counterparts in payload capacity and operational flexibility.” Official specs list a payload capacity of 10-plus tons for this cargo UGV, and a driving range comparable to that of the Bushmaster’s 600-plus kilometers.
The Bushmaster’s original mechanicals have been replaced by a hybrid energy and battery storage solution from 3ME Technology, Thales Australia’s partner in the effort.
For the BladeHaul the company has assembled a 660V power system that offers 110kWh of power.

Justin Bain, CEO of 3ME Technology, said: “Working with Thales Australia brings together the best of Australian innovation, combining 3ME Technology’s systems engineering and platform development capabilities with the Bushmaster’s proven performance and established manufacturing base.

Together we’re delivering an entirely new XL-UGV at a time when demand for contested logistics and remote power solutions for littoral environments is present and growing.” Thales Australia envisages three potential use cases for the BladeHaul: as a cargo mover in zones of contested logistics; as a mobile and enduring power source for other equipment; and as a highly mobile platform for sensors and effectors.

Thales Australia said in a statement: “By integrating advanced autonomy that enables human-machine teaming, hybrid technology, heavy payload capacity and power generation within a single platform, Thales Australia and 3ME Technology are delivering a next-generation solution that enhances operational readiness and supports Australia’s commitment to sovereign defense innovation.” The BladeHaul is aimed at the Australian Army, but its appeal extends to any land force, according to the manufacturer.

items.title: Skapion launches counter drone swarm C-UAS system designed to engage 100 targets
items.originalTitle: Skapion launches counter drone swarm C-UAS system designed to engage 100 targets
items.summary: Skapion, a defence technology company developing advanced counter-swarm solutions, has unveiled what the company calls “the world’s first native counter-swarm defence system” – a new class of air-defense capability purpose-built from the ground up to detect, engage and defeat large-scale, coordinated drone swarm attacks, in an affordable cost. Skapion recently announced a USD36 million Seed funding round led by UP. Partners and Khosla Ventures to accelerate the development and validation of its counter-swarm defense system.

evidenceRecords.text: Skapion, a defence technology company developing advanced counter-swarm solutions, has unveiled what the company calls “the world’s first native counter-swarm defence system” – a new class of air-defense capability purpose-built from the ground up to detect, engage and defeat large-scale, coordinated drone swarm attacks, in an affordable cost.
Partners and Khosla Ventures to accelerate the development and validation of its counter-swarm defense system.

The company’s system has been designed by Skapion’s Founding Architect, General (ret.) Pini Yungman, Architect of Iron Dome and former GM of Rafael Air & Missile Defense and engineered from inception around a native many-to-many architecture, enabling multiple interceptors to engage multiple targets simultaneously and at scale, said the company in a press release.

“The highly mobile, fully kinetic system is designed to simultaneously engage more than 100 targets with an interception rate above 97%, while delivering a significantly lower cost per interception compared with conventional air-defense solutions – creating an economically sustainable defense layer against mass, low-cost aerial threats,” said Skapion.
At the center of the system is an AI command-and-control architecture that fuses data from Skapion’s own detection and tracking sensors or third-party systems.
It evaluates and prioritizes threats, allocates interceptors and manages engagements in real time – allowing full end-to-end autonomy or a single human operator on the loop – per customer policy.
Skapion recently announced a USD36 million Seed funding round led by UP.
An open, sensor-agnostic architecture enables integration with external threat data, existing C2 systems and other counter-UAS systems.

items.title: Ukraine races to field faster interceptors as Russia hammers its energy grid
items.originalTitle: Ukraine races to field faster interceptors as Russia hammers its energy grid
items.summary: KYIV, Ukraine — Russia is still using fast jet-powered drones to batter Ukraine’s energy facilities, bridges and other critical infrastructure at speeds beyond the reach of most of Kyiv’s drone interceptors, despite U.S. President Donald Trump’s unilateral announcement on Sunday of an energy ceasefire between the two countries. Russia began using the jets heavily in July, when their numbers jumped fivefold from the previous month.

evidenceRecords.text: KYIV, Ukraine — Russia is still using fast jet-powered drones to batter Ukraine’s energy facilities, bridges and other critical infrastructure at speeds beyond the reach of most of Kyiv’s drone interceptors, despite U.S. President Donald Trump’s unilateral announcement on Sunday of an energy ceasefire between the two countries.
Russia began using the jets heavily in July, when their numbers jumped fivefold from the previous month.

They can now reach speeds of up to 373 mph (600 km/h) — more than three times the speed of the propeller-driven Geran-2 drones they evolved from — far exceeding the top velocity of the average Ukrainian interceptor drone, air force officials told lawmakers last week.
To stop the drones, Ukraine must instead rely on F-16s, newly installed machine gun turrets that use artificial intelligence to aim and costly air-defense missiles that are in short supply globally.
“Ukraine did not strike Russian oil refining and the energy sector in general for two days after the American president announced a ceasefire in the energy sector.

But Russia did not listen to the American president,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote after jets seriously damaged a gas production facility in the northeastern Kharkiv region on Sunday night.
Russia launched 167 missiles and drones overnight Tuesday into Wednesday, including 77 jet-powered drones, which officials said struck one of Kyiv’s main power plants and left 600,000 without power.

Ukraine’s Air Force says they are beginning to field more effective countermeasures, but with Russia continuing to optimize the design of jet-powered drones to destroy critical infrastructure, the development of jets and anti-jet interceptors has become the latest neck-and-neck technology race on the battlefield.

Iran shipped Russia its first Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 drones in mid-August 2022, and Moscow rebranded them the Geran-1 and Geran-2 and was firing them at Ukrainian civilian infrastructure by that October.

Those propeller-driven drones were slow enough for Ukraine to build an economical defense around mobile fire teams and cheap interceptor drones rather than spending scarce missiles on every Shahed, and in February the interceptors accounted for more than 70% of Shahed downings over Kyiv .

items.title: Sikorsky’s Nomad 100 VTOL Drone Is Now Quad-Packed In A Container For Rapid Deployment
items.originalTitle: Sikorsky’s Nomad 100 VTOL Drone Is Now Quad-Packed In A Container For Rapid Deployment
items.summary: Sikorsky has unveiled a concept for a containerized deployment package for its Nomad 100 vertical takeoff and landing uncrewed aircraft system (VTOL UAS), combining four aircraft and their support equipment inside a single 20-foot shipping container. The company is pitching the Nomad 100 Fast Pack as a way to rapidly establish autonomous air capabilities at locations without runways or other conventional support infrastructure. The concept was unveiled on October 12 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention in Washington, D.C., where TWZ is in attendance.

evidenceRecords.text: Sikorsky has unveiled a concept for a containerized deployment package for its Nomad 100 vertical takeoff and landing uncrewed aircraft system (VTOL UAS), combining four aircraft and their support equipment inside a single 20-foot shipping container.
The company is pitching the Nomad 100 Fast Pack as a way to rapidly establish autonomous air capabilities at locations without runways or other conventional support infrastructure.
The concept was unveiled on October 12 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention in Washington, D.C., where TWZ is in attendance.

It comes as the U.S. military seeks to expand its inventory of uncrewed systems and distribute capabilities across more dispersed operating locations, particularly in preparation for a potential large-scale conflict with China in the Indo-Pacific.
Rendering of the Nomad 100 Fast Pack in action.

Courtesy of Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company Rendering courtesy of Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company “Military commanders are asking for capability that enables them to deploy worldwide into austere environments,” said Ramsey Bentley, director of Sikorsky Advanced Concepts, speaking at AUSA.
They want greater situational awareness, the ability to conduct targeting and deliver effects at range, and the capacity to control multiple assets simultaneously, he added.
Sikorsky screencap The Nomad 100 Fast Pack is built around a standard 20-foot ISO container housing four aircraft, mission-command equipment, communications, power systems, and sustainment supplies.
A promotional video shows the Fast Pack being transported into a combat theater by one of the company’s Black Hawk helicopters as a slung load.

Sikorsky says two Nomad 100s can be prepared for flight “out of the box” in less than 15 minutes and that the other two aircraft — stored on the upper shelf of the container — can be made available within four to six hours.
The package is designed to support runway-independent operations from locations including naval vessels, tactical vehicle staging areas, and improvised landing zones.

As we have discussed in the past , the Nomad 100 combines vertical takeoff and landing with the ability to transition to fixed-wing flight, bringing airplane-like range and endurance to a compact, runway-independent package that can operate from confined locations.

The test, expected in the coming months, will also give the Artemis III crew their first full launch-day rehearsal on the pad ahead of the targeted no-earlier-than June 2027 mission.

Engineers with NASA’s Exploration Ground Systems finished stacking the twin five-segment boosters on September 30 by mating the aerodynamic nose cones to the left and right forward assemblies inside the Vehicle Assembly Building’s High Bay 3 at Kennedy Space Center.
The boosters, built by Northrop Grumman, will deliver more than 75 percent of total SLS thrust at liftoff from Pad 39B.
NASA plans to roll the short stack to Launch Pad 39B for a tanking test, during which the launch team will practice propellant loading timelines and procedures.

evidenceRecords.text: Türkiye’s domestically developed MALAMAN smart bottom mine was deployed during the multinational Nusret 2026 mine warfare exercise, marking another operational milestone for the system.
Hosted by Türkiye from October 6 to 16 in the Gulf of Izmir and off Karadeniz Ereğli in the Black Sea, the Nusret 2026 Invitation Exercise provided the operational backdrop for the demonstration.
During the exercise, a MALAMAN mine was seen being laid from the Turkish Navy’s Tuzla-class patrol boat TCG Karabiga (P-1205).
Wrapped in artificial grass camouflage designed to mimic seabed vegetation, the mine was launched into the water from the ship’s stern.
MALAMAN was developed through a joint defense industry effort involving KoçSavunma, MKE, and TÜBİTAK SAGE to address the Turkish Navy’s modern mine warfare requirements.
According to details released by the Turkish Ministry of National Defence, Nusret 2026 brings together 20 naval vessels, five aircraft, and various unmanned systems.
Turkish Naval Forces, Air Force, and Coast Guard units are participating alongside NATO and partner nations.

Key participant groups include NATO’s Standing Mine Countermeasures Group 2 (SNMCMG2)—with assets from Germany, Greece, Italy, Spain, and Türkiye—and the Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Task Group, featuring ships from Bulgaria, Romania, and Türkiye.
The exercise focuses on the planning, execution, and evaluation of mine warfare operations, emphasizing interoperability in multi-threat environments.

About the MALAMAN Smart Mine A mockup of Malaman Smart Sea Mine exhibited at DSA 2024 in Malaysia MALAMAN is a seabed/bottom mine equipped with acoustic, magnetic and pressure sensors for target detection and classification.

items.title: France mulls keeping Charles de Gaulle carrier sailing after 2038
items.originalTitle: France mulls keeping Charles de Gaulle carrier sailing after 2038
items.summary: PARIS — France is studying whether the Charles de Gaulle nuclear-powered aircraft carrier can continue to sail beyond its envisaged retirement in 2038, which would give the country a fleet of two carriers, French Navy Chief of Staff Adm. Christophe Cluzel told lawmakers in a hearing here on Wednesday. The French Navy plans to replace the Charles de Gaulle, the only nuclear-powered aircraft carrier in operation outside the United States Navy, with a future carrier to be named France Libre in 2038.

evidenceRecords.text: PARIS — France is studying whether the Charles de Gaulle nuclear-powered aircraft carrier can continue to sail beyond its envisaged retirement in 2038, which would give the country a fleet of two carriers, French Navy Chief of Staff Adm.
Christophe Cluzel told lawmakers in a hearing here on Wednesday.
The French Navy plans to replace the Charles de Gaulle, the only nuclear-powered aircraft carrier in operation outside the United States Navy, with a future carrier to be named France Libre in 2038.
As part of an upcoming major refit, France will look into whether the Charles de Gaulle can continue to operate longer, based on the state of onboard systems and the nuclear propulsion, Cluzel said.

With a single carrier, France is without one any time the Charles de Gaulle is in dock for periodic maintenance, and the issue of whether the country needs a second carrier tends to pop up whenever lawmakers question Navy brass.
One obstacle is cost, with the estimated €10 billion budget (US$11.2 billion) for the future France Libre carrier enough to fund at least ten new FDI-class frigates.
Two carriers allow you to maintain a standing alert from Toulon,” Cluzel told the National Assembly’s defense committee, referring to the Charles de Gaulle’s home port in southern France.

He said the future France Libre and the Charles de Gaulle will have two years of overlap in 2036-2038, with two aircraft-carrier crews on active duty, which the Navy chief said is necessary for a seamless transition of skills.

“So from 2036 to 2038 there is a period when the Navy will again have two carriers able to be at sea simultaneously. ”France has said the France Libre will measure 310 meters and displace about 80,000 tonnes, compared to 261.5 meters and 42,000 tons for the Charles de Gaulle.

Studies on extending the Charles de Gaulle’s service life will look at the wear on the reactor cores at the heart of the carrier’s nuclear propulsion system, and the ability to extend operations by keeping fuel on board the carrier for longer, according to Cluzel.

France is committed to limiting its dependencies, and similar to what it did for the steam-powered catapults on the Charles de Gaulle, the country will buy a “substantial” inventory of spare parts for its electromagnetic catapults right at the start of the program, to ensure it can perform repairs independently, according to Cluzel.

Skills and Training Building advanced intelligence capability across Europe requires knowledge that travels as freely as compute.

The NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute has launched a new open source courseware hub with hands-on course materials covering accelerated computing and deep learning — freely downloadable and openly licensed, with no enrollment, fees or deadline.

Modular by design, the courses can be adapted for university curricula, supercomputing center bootcamps or developer community events, and serve as a direct bridge to NVIDIA’s broader training and certification programs .

items.summary: Leonardo DRS has been awarded an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) contract with a ceiling value of USD500 million by the US Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF-401) to support counter-unmanned aircraft systems (C-UAS) missions. The contract has a three-year period of performance and is intended to accelerate the delivery of vetted C-UAS technologies to military operators. Under the agreement, Leonardo DRS will be eligible to compete for task orders to supply integrated sensing capabilities for force protection and low-altitude air defence.

items.title: F-35C Makes First Arrested Landing Aboard A Ford Class Carrier
items.originalTitle: F-35C Makes First Arrested Landing Aboard A Ford Class Carrier
items.summary: A U.S. Navy F-35C has made the first arrested landing for the type aboard a Ford class aircraft carrier, with the milestone taking place aboard the future USS John F. The milestone marks a major step in testing the Navy’s stealth fighter aboard its newest carrier class, following years of challenges integrating advanced launch and recovery systems. Two F-35C test pilots assigned to Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 23 (VX-23), part of the Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division (NAWCAD), flew to the carrier as part of an ongoing Aircraft Compatibility Testing (ACT) campaign.

items.title: Hegseth, service secretaries discuss ‘generational change’ of Autonomous Warfare Command
items.originalTitle: Hegseth, service secretaries discuss ‘generational change’ of Autonomous Warfare Command
items.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s vision for the planned Autonomous Warfare Command over the next two years “is that we're still iterating, we're still adapting, we're still learning, and we're moving faster and faster because we're doing it. The secretary, who has ordered cuts to and flag officer positions across the military services, was asked why a four-star combatant command is the correct vehicle to speed up acquisition and fielding of autonomous systems. “Let's put rank where we need it to ensure we can drive change quickly,” Hegseth said.

evidenceRecords.text: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s vision for the planned Autonomous Warfare Command over the next two years “is that we're still iterating, we're still adapting, we're still learning, and we're moving faster and faster because we're doing it.

We understand how to do it better with each iteration.” Hegseth sat down to discuss the Defense Department’s efforts to advance its autonomous capabilities with the service secretaries and the Pentagon’s top civilian for special operations during a panel Wednesday at AUSA’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C., but the discussion offered few details on what the forthcoming AUTOWARCOM, scheduled to activate by Oct. 1, 2027, will look like and how it will accomplish its mission.

The secretary, who has ordered cuts to and flag officer positions across the military services, was asked why a four-star combatant command is the correct vehicle to speed up acquisition and fielding of autonomous systems.
“Let's put rank where we need it to ensure we can drive change quickly,” Hegseth said.

“We're going to use rank to drive change with the right people in those positions, but not just legacy formations and commands which have gathered over time and haven't led to battlefield efforts.” He did not say whether a search is on for commander candidates and what kind of experience he’s looking for.

He did not say whether a search is on for commander candidates and what kind of experience he\u2019s looking for.\u00a0

The Army on Tuesday announced it would rename its Futures and Concepts Command, headed by Lt. Gen. Mac McCurry, to Futures and Autonomy Command, which will be the service\u2019s component command nested under AUTOWARCOM.
The other services haven\u2019t made any announcements about their own forthcoming autonomy commands.
The Navy did not immediately respond to a query from Defense One on its plans.
The Air Force referred questions to Hegseth\u2019s office.\u00a0
Much of the discussion focused on the services\u2019 current use of unmanned platforms, as distinct from autonomous systems, which generally function without a human operator.

Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on Thursday said that his country's military had resumed strikes on Russian energy infrastructure despite US President Donald Trump's insistence that such attacks stop.
Zelenskyy made the statement in an interview with London's Financial Times (FT) newspaper, saying: "The block [on energy infrastructure attacks] is out.
We're done."
Kyiv had refrained from making attacks to give Trump's "energy ceasefire" a chance for success.

On Thursday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised "vigorous [US] efforts to initiate the peace process," and claimed that by resuming attacks, Ukraine "is coming into serious conflict with the peace efforts of the United States and American negotiators."

Russia, however, has paid no heed to Trump, instead continuing to hit Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure, for instance on Wednesday, when Russian strikes cut power to 600,000 Ukrainian citizens.
Ukraine had gone along with Trump's public proposal — despite not being notified of any "ceasefire" ahead of time — but it seemed to have helped little in the eyes of US leadership.

To that end, Zelenskyy railed against a "dangerous" lack of US intelligence information this week as well as the throttling of SpaceX Starlink satellite access for Ukraine's troops after Trump last week announced a number of decisions that have had adverse consequences for Ukraine.
The Ukrainian president said his country's military leaders had been warned that they would not be receiving US intelligence if they did not abide by Trump's "ceasefire."
Despite Ukraine's restraint, that withholding of intelligence was on full display this week when Kyiv was blindsided by Russian drones and missiles without any prior warning from the US.
"We will find a way out," said Zelenskyy of the situation as Ukraine's Western allies scramble to pick up the intelligence and defensive slack left by the US.

Zelenskyy said he would be willing to halt energy infrastructure attacks again but only if the US supplied Patriot interceptors that would allow Kyiv to down incoming the Russian ballistic missiles and drones that have been raining down on Ukraine since February 24, 2022.
Despite US claims that the Starlink situation was the result of a technical glitch, Zelenskyy told the FT, "It was not a technical problem, it was will."

PRESS RELEASE — ZeroTier , one of the world’s top software-defined networking companies, today announced Release Candidate 3 (RC3) of ZeroTier Quantum, the world’s only software-defined end-to-end quantum-secure networking platform.
RC3 moves ZeroTier Quantum closer to production readiness through expanded flexibility, broader client support, stronger administrative controls, and continued testing and platform hardening.

When it comes to defense, government, finance, critical infrastructure, and enterprise environments, flexibility means deploying quantum-secure networking in a way that fits existing architecture, security requirements, and operational needs, without a rip-and-replace approach.
“With RC3, we’re proving that quantum-secure connectivity can adapt to the environments organizations actually operate in.

We have significant experience in this regard, and our customers can deploy ZeroTier Quantum across managed, sovereign, and isolated environments, including systems that never touch the public internet.” Fully Quantum-Secure Connectivity Under Customer Control Additionally RC3 represents a significant validation milestone for ZeroTier Quantum, strengthening the platform across not only deployment flexibility, but also security, access control, performance and operational readiness.
The RC3 includes: Quantum-safe cryptography built in: ZeroTier Quantum combines ML-KEM-1024 with optional P-384 classical cryptography in a configurable hybrid key exchange.
Together, these capabilities move ZeroTier Quantum well beyond core functional validation and continue to establish it as a ready high-performance, highly secure, and flexible networking platform.
“We’ve been very deliberate in our development of ZeroTier Quantum around real customer requirements, both real-world networking challenges and regulatory roadmap pressure.
RC3 is already in use with live customers with strict requirements around cryptography, isolation, and/or control,” said Robert Stevenson, ZeroTier’s Chief Commercial Officer.

“What we’re seeing is demand for quantum-secure networking that organizations of all sizes can deploy on their own terms, within their own environments, while still preserving the integrity of their years, even decades of prior work.” A Major Step Toward Production-Ready Quantum Security RC3 also marks a major validation milestone for ZeroTier Quantum in terms of production hardening.

evidenceRecords.text: ANRA Technologies has introduced VISTA (Visual Interface for Shared Traffic Awareness), an application designed to give public safety agencies and commercial drone operators greater awareness of nearby drone activity through information available from UAS traffic management (UTM) services.
The application displays available flight intentions and reported positions, helping operators understand what other aircraft may be operating nearby before and during a mission.
It does not require changes to existing drones, flight applications or operating procedures.
VISTA is designed to complement existing safety procedures rather than detect every drone in the sky.

The receive-only application does not connect aircraft to UTM services or submit flight plans, instead providing an additional layer of airspace awareness based on information available through the UTM ecosystem.

ANRA said its UTM platform supports approximately one drone mission every 15 seconds during daytime operations, while more than 20 organisations, primarily Drone as First Responder (DFR) programmes, already use its visualisation capabilities.
The company said VISTA is intended to help public safety agencies coordinate drone operations near emergency scenes, while also supporting enterprise activities such as infrastructure inspections.
ANRA is offering demonstrations to organisations interested in the application.

items.originalTitle: SAXON Q Reports That Room-Temperature Quantum Computers Can Rival the Performance of Superconducting Processors
items.summary: Insider Brief SAXON Q reported that its room-temperature diamond quantum computer achieved 77.3% success in a three-qubit Grover search, close to the cited superconducting benchmark of 78%. The system achieved 87% success when searching for two targets among eight items, with both tests exceeding the classical success limits cited in the paper. evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief SAXON Q reported that its room-temperature diamond quantum computer achieved 77.3% success in a three-qubit Grover search, close to the cited superconducting benchmark of 78%.
The system achieved 87% success when searching for two targets among eight items, with both tests exceeding the classical success limits cited in the paper.
Researchers conducted the benchmark at Fraunhofer IWU in Dresden using a previous-generation system that consumes roughly 600 watts and requires no cryogenic cooling or vacuum equipment.

PRESS RELEASE — — SAXON Q , a leader in NV-center quantum computing, today released a paper showing that its room-temperature diamond-based system can perform on par with superconducting quantum computers cooled to near absolute zero.

Running Grover’s search algorithm, a standard benchmark test for quantum performance, a SAXON Q system identified a single target state 77.3% of the time using three qubits, rivaling the best published superconducting result of 78%, which required a temperature roughly 15,000 times colder.
“The assumption in quantum computing has been that you trade performance for convenience.

“Our system ran a complete quantum algorithm in an ordinary room at a customer site, and the results were similar to those of machines that require extensive infrastructure to cool them to near absolute zero.” Grover’s algorithm — also known as the “quantum search algorithm” — has been used for years to benchmark quantum computers.

It finds a marked item in an unsorted list, using fewer steps than any classical computing method can, and it is a building block for how quantum applications will approach optimization work, financial analysis, cryptography and more.
It uses a sequence that includes the qubits, single and multi-qubit gates, repeated operations and a final readout, all of which work together.

Superconducting quantum computers, by contrast, can demand upwards of 25 kilowatts and must be cooled to near absolute zero inside dilution refrigerators that require specialized facilities and chilled-water cooling.
The experiment was conducted on a previous-generation SAXON Q quantum computer, which predates its new SXQ128 and SXQ512 quantum computers announced in July.
The SXQ128 is available to order now , and SXQ512 deliveries are scheduled to begin in the second quarter of 2027.

items.summary: Insider Brief ORCA Computing launched its PT-3 photonic quantum computer at Digital Realty’s London innovation lab, pairing it with NVIDIA accelerated computing for scientific AI and industrial optimization. evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief ORCA Computing launched its PT-3 photonic quantum computer at Digital Realty’s London innovation lab, pairing it with NVIDIA accelerated computing for scientific AI and industrial optimization.
ORCA said the PT-3 completed a hybrid energy-scheduling workflow in about an hour, more than 12 times faster than its predecessor at the same solution quality.

PRESS RELEASE — ORCA Computing , the company pioneering quantum-accelerated AI for science, today launches the PT-3, the newest generation of its photonic quantum computers, and the first built to deliver commercial quantum advantage.

ORCA’s PT-3 works alongside GPUs to increase the expressivity of AI models (their ability to represent complex patterns and data distributions), helping them learn more from limited data and identify better, more novel candidates for new drugs and materials.
Already delivering results The PT-3 has allowed ORCA to generate results from a hybrid quantum-classical extension of NVIDIA Proteína , the generative model for protein design.

Trained on 32 NVIDIA Hopper GPUs working with a PT-3 using 64 photons in 128 qumodes, the hybrid model showed enhanced designability over the classical baseline, improving the ratio of useful proteins by 20%, and generated novel proteins with a different mix of secondary structures.
The PT-3 is also being applied to optimisation problems such as smarter energy scheduling.

Earlier this year, JIJ Inc. and ORCA, in collaboration with bp and the UK’s National Quantum Computing Centre (NQCC), published a white paper that benchmarked hybrid approaches to the unit commitment problem.
On that 25,755-variable benchmark, ORCA’s PT-3 now runs the hybrid quantum-classical workflow in about an hour, more than 12× faster than its predecessor at the same solution quality.

Richard Murray, Co-founder and CEO of ORCA Computing, said: “By integrating our photonic quantum computer with NVIDIA accelerated computing, we have taken a critical first step in the future of hybrid quantum supercomputing.

items.title: Riverlane and NVIDIA Use AI to Speed Up Quantum Decoder Calibration
items.originalTitle: Riverlane and NVIDIA Use AI to Speed Up Quantum Decoder Calibration
items.summary: Insider Brief Riverlane and NVIDIA are exploring how AI and GPU-accelerated computing can speed up decoder calibration for quantum error correction as quantum hardware behaviour changes. Using Riverlane ’s Local Clustering Decoder on an NVIDIA H100 GPU, the reported surface-code training cycle fell from three minutes on a single CPU core to 2.8 seconds. The H100 processed more than four million surface-code syndromes per second in the reported tests, compared with around 59,000 per second on a single CPU core, supporting more frequent decoder recalibration.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Riverlane and NVIDIA are exploring how AI and GPU-accelerated computing can speed up decoder calibration for quantum error correction as quantum hardware behaviour changes.
Using Riverlane ’s Local Clustering Decoder on an NVIDIA H100 GPU, the reported surface-code training cycle fell from three minutes on a single CPU core to 2.8 seconds.

The H100 processed more than four million surface-code syndromes per second in the reported tests, compared with around 59,000 per second on a single CPU core, supporting more frequent decoder recalibration.
PRESS RELEASE — Quantum computing has the potential to solve problems beyond the reach of today’s computers, from drug discovery to materials science and optimisation.
But before that can happen, the industry must first overcome the errors that are created by quantum computing’s extreme sensitivity to noise.
Quantum error correction (QEC) detects and corrects these errors.
It’s essential for building reliable and useful quantum computers, but this also creates enormous demands for real-time data processing.
Future systems may need to process terabytes of information every second, with near-perfect accuracy, to support error-free quantum computing.

To explore how to meet these demands, Riverlane and NVIDIA are collaborating on the use of AI and NVIDIA accelerated computing for QEC, including how GPUs can make decoder calibration faster, and help quantum systems keep up with changes in hardware behaviour.
Keeping up with Changing Quantum Hardware A decoder is the part of a QEC system that interprets the signals produced by a quantum processor.
Building a Faster and More Efficient Calibration Loop Riverlane has developed an AI-based calibration loop that learns improved decoder settings directly from experimental data.
As part of a collaboration, Riverlane uses NVIDIA H100 GPU to test how well different decoder settings perform.

items.summary: Within the 2nd Cavalry Regiment, or 2CR, new basics include unmanned aerial systems operation and employment, counter-UAS systems and unmanned ground vehicle usage, service officials said during a Monday discussion at the Association of the U.S. Army annual meeting , titled “ Project Flytrap —Accelerating Offensive Maneuver through Data-Centric Kill Web.” Project Flytrap is an Army counter-unmanned aerial systems initiative and multinational exercise, which has leveled up from the individual soldier to the squadron level with multiple iterations.

evidenceRecords.text: Within the 2nd Cavalry Regiment, or 2CR, new basics include unmanned aerial systems operation and employment, counter-UAS systems and unmanned ground vehicle usage, service officials said during a Monday discussion at the Association of the U.S. Army annual meeting , titled “ Project Flytrap —Accelerating Offensive Maneuver through Data-Centric Kill Web.” Project Flytrap is an Army counter-unmanned aerial systems initiative and multinational exercise, which has leveled up from the individual soldier to the squadron level with multiple iterations.

The most recent exercise, Project Flytrap 5.0, took place in Lithuania and was concluded earlier this year with partner nations, including the United Kingdom and Australia, and was led by the Army’s V Corps .
The countries integrated and tested more than 50 industry-provided technologies, launched effects and unmanned ground vehicles and tested against a live opposing force.
“The American way of war is centered on maneuver, and counter-UAS cannot remain tied to static defense,” Col.
Timothy Price, commander of the 2nd Cavalry Regiment, said in a Tuesday release .

“Project FlyTrap ensures we maintain mobility and offensive survivability in a highly contested, opaque operational environment.” The 2nd Cavalry Regiment is expanding Project Flytrap into a battalion-level operational capability, adapting from small-unit field trials into tactical employment connected with operational objectives aimed at breaking through drone-saturated frontlines on Europe’s Eastern Flank.
“As we’re training our soldiers for the multi-domain operations, or multi-domain breeds, we talk about the new basics inside of 2CR,” Command Sgt.
Jesse Clark, 2nd Cavalry Regiment senior enlisted leader, said during Monday’s discussion.

“With the new basics, we need to focus on sUAS, counter-UAS, camouflage for electromagnetic signatures … and how we’re going to do that so soldiers understand how to camouflage themselves with those spectrum options,” he continued.
Officials listed the previous basics to include topics such as marksmanship, map reading and navigation, radio etiquette and UAS and jamming reaction to contact.
Clark said the service needs to have disciplined unit training management in which personnel, time and equipment are included to ensure soldiers are proficient at the new basics.

Moscow said two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port were hit during the sea crossing.
It did not name the vessels.
On Tuesday, two merchant ships were struck by drones further south along the coast of Bulgaria, Romania's neighbour, and one of the vessels sank, leaving 11 crew members missing.
Bulgaria said it suspected Russia was behind that attack, summoning the country's envoy.
A search and rescue operation for the eight missing members of the Wine Trader continues, Romania's authorities have said.
Two Black Hawk helicopters and two rescue boats have been deployed.
The priority is now to reach the four crew members confirmed to be alive, while ensuring the safety of rescue teams with very high waves reported in the area.

items.summary: Australia’s Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) will continue its broad-area beyond visual line-of-sight (BVLOS) drone trial while developing a long-term approach to these operations. Following an internal review, CASA is working on an enduring framework that builds on the existing trial arrangements, which provide eligible operators with more flexible pathways to conduct BVLOS flights across larger areas. The regulator expects to open public consultation in November 2026 on draft guidance for broad-area BVLOS operations.

evidenceRecords.text: Australia’s Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) will continue its broad-area beyond visual line-of-sight (BVLOS) drone trial while developing a long-term approach to these operations.

Following an internal review, CASA is working on an enduring framework that builds on the existing trial arrangements, which provide eligible operators with more flexible pathways to conduct BVLOS flights across larger areas.
The regulator expects to open public consultation in November 2026 on draft guidance for broad-area BVLOS operations.
CASA will seek industry feedback to ensure the guidance is clear and practical for operators applying for broad-area BVLOS approvals.
Existing trial arrangements will remain in place until a long-term solution is established, allowing eligible operators to continue using the current pathways.
The proposed guidance will form Annex B to Advisory Circular AC 101-06 and build on the pathways introduced through the trial.

evidenceRecords.text: Defense autonomy startup Rownd has secured a $10 million contract with the Department of War as it develops low-cost, autonomous drones designed for military operations.
The company is also expanding its operations in Wisconsin and North Carolina, adding jobs and investing in drone research and development.
Headquartered in Raleigh, NC, Rownd is focused on what the defense industry calls attritable mass: deploying drones that are affordable enough to be replaced if lost in combat.
The approach aims to give military forces more autonomous systems without relying on expensive platforms that are difficult to replace.
Rownd’s technology is designed to let drones process information and make decisions onboard rather than depend on constant cloud connectivity or centralized ground control.
Its AI software also enables drones to communicate and coordinate with one another, including when a swarm loses its connection to external networks.
The company recently put those capabilities to the test during a three-day exercise with Air Force personnel in Alabama.
Rownd’s quadcopters completed 41 flights, including four mobile flights and four fleet tests using onboard AI.
The exercise also marked the company’s first drone swarm demonstration, with up to three aircraft flying simultaneously.
Rownd used the exercise to demonstrate another part of its development process: improving its AI models using real-world flight data.
Each night, the team retrained the drones’ computer-vision models using data collected during the day’s flights and uploaded the updated models before the next day’s missions.
According to the company, this process significantly improved accuracy.

items.originalTitle: NYC Awards $29.2 million to New York University to Establish a Cutting-edge Quantum Fabrication Facility
items.summary: New York City will award NYU $29.2 million to establish a quantum fabrication facility, backed by an additional $255 million from the university and expected to open in 2030. The city will receive three advisory board seats and 15% of NYU Central Administration’s proceeds from intellectual property created using city-funded equipment. QFab will provide quantum device manufacturing and testing, startup support and workforce training, with plans to reach more than 35,000 New Yorkers during its first decade.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief New York City will award NYU $29.2 million to establish a quantum fabrication facility, backed by an additional $255 million from the university and expected to open in 2030.
New York City will award NYU $29.2 million to establish a quantum fabrication facility, backed by an additional $255 million from the university and expected to open in 2030.
The city will receive three advisory board seats and 15% of NYU Central Administration’s proceeds from intellectual property created using city-funded equipment.
QFab will provide quantum device manufacturing and testing, startup support and workforce training, with plans to reach more than 35,000 New Yorkers during its first decade.

PRESS RELEASE — Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani, Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice Julie Su and New York City Economic Development Corporation (NYCEDC) President and CEO Anthony Shorris announced the city will award $29.2 million to New York University to establish a cutting-edge Quantum Fabrication Facility (QFab), putting New York City at the front of the emerging quantum technology field.

As part of the Mamdani administration’s investment, the city will receive board seats at QFab as well as a stake in new technologies that emerge from QFab, a first-of-its-kind agreement that will allow the City to help shape this emerging technology for the public good.

QFab — which is backed by an additional $255 million investment from NYU spanning construction and 10 years of operations — will give researchers, students, start-ups and established companies access to specialized equipment for building and testing new quantum devices.
It is expected to support more than 100 companies and reach 35,000 New Yorkers in its first 10 years of operation.

Additionally, to grow the number of New York City jobs in the quantum field, NYU will provide students at the City University of New York (CUNY) and New York City Public Schools (NYCPS) with access to state-of-the-art labs, training, new certificate programs and summer workshops.

Altogether, today’s announcement represents a historic investment by the Mamdani administration in the future of New York City’s economy and helps set a new national model for economic development for the public good.

“Providing New York City students, researchers, and companies with access to a Quantum Fabrication Facility (QFab) and specialized equipment through NYU will allow our City to engage, shape, and grow with this emerging technology,” said Assemblymember Deborah Glick.

items.title: US Army taps 9 companies to build next-gen command and control software
items.originalTitle: US Army taps 9 companies to build next-gen command and control software
items.summary: The U.S. Army announced that it is awarding initial contracts to several defense technology companies to build applications for its new battlefield software. The service will pay a one-year total of $93.6 million, spread out across nine companies, to create applications for its Next Generation Command and Control, or NGC2, software. “While the Army is providing capability we can deploy today, we’re also providing a blueprint and reference point for how industry can integrate in the future with interoperability and speed,” said Brig.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army announced that it is awarding initial contracts to several defense technology companies to build applications for its new battlefield software.
The service will pay a one-year total of $93.6 million, spread out across nine companies, to create applications for its Next Generation Command and Control, or NGC2, software.

The NGC2 system, in conjunction with the applications the companies build for it, will allow information sharing that streamlines mission completion across the Army’s six warfighting functions of command and control, fires, intelligence, movement and maneuver, sustainment and protection, the service said.

“While the Army is providing capability we can deploy today, we’re also providing a blueprint and reference point for how industry can integrate in the future with interoperability and speed,” said Brig.
Gen. Shane Taylor, portfolio management executive for the Command and Control Information Network.
The NGC2 will provide a shared network for technologies, weapons, sensors, devices and applications to operate within that will increase decision-making speed on the battlefield.
The chosen companies include General Dynamics Mission Systems, Air Space Intelligence Federal, Immersive Wisdom, LMI, Mente Systems, Stilman Advanced Strategies, Onebrief, Rune Technologies and AIR.
The applications will be hosted on the common data baseline, or software foundation, that Anduril Industries, Palantir, Raft and Striveworks have built in collaboration with the Army.
The Army is currently in the process of delivering the NGC2 software to the I Corps, which commands service members in the Indo-Pacific.
The move will further test NGC2 software’s ability to host technologies and devices separated by thousands of miles, some in communication-contested environments.

The Army has spent the last year moving from the experimental phase to the fielding phase of NGC2, going from prototype development to placing software in the hands of soldiers at the 4th and 25th Infantry Divisions.

In July 2026, the Army hosted a 10-day event at Fort Irwin, California, entitled Project Convergence-Capstone 6, that asked 10,000 participants from U.S. and allied forces as well as industry partners using 90 technologies to test software for the NGC2.

evidenceRecords.text: Jérôme Botoko Ekila, a doctoral student at the VUB's AI Lab, explains, "Instead of forcing AI systems to communicate in a human language that does not correspond to their sensors, we allow them to develop their own 'artificial natural language.' They construct effective concepts that correspond exactly to what they perceive via their sensors, even if the data is incomprehensible to humans."
Because sensors on different machines or vehicles can never be calibrated identically in practice, the researchers believe that this language offers the ideal solution.

Paul Van Eecke, a professor of artificial intelligence at the VUB, says, "In industrial or physical applications, it is simply unrealistic to expect all the sensors on different robots or vehicles to be calibrated in exactly the same way.
"Humans solve this problem through language: if I say I am standing near the 'red car,' we understand each other without our eyes registering exactly the same color values.
Language provides a layer of abstraction above the sensor readings, and this is precisely what we are now allowing these AI agents to construct autonomously."

Instead of preprogrammed words or fixed codes, the researchers provided the agents with the basic mechanisms underpinning the evolution of human language: the local invention of words, the adaptation of conceptual prototypes and the incorporation of feedback following successful or failed communication.
Katrien Beuls, a professor at UNamur, explains, "What's fascinating is that there's no central computer imposing the rules.
Each time, we let two agents communicate with one another at a local level.
It is solely through these individual interactions and updates that a global convention emerges spontaneously across the entire population.
The universal applicability of the method has been demonstrated across 37 varied and complex data sets.
The agents successfully developed their own vocabulary to communicate, notably regarding physicochemical analyses of wine, NASA data on exoplanets, visual data sets and images of birds or faces.
In all these situations, the agents successfully synthesized the data into new, shared concepts.

evidenceRecords.text: The article Anthropic's Q3 revenue hits $16.8B but growth slows ahead of planned November IPO appeared first on The Decoder .
Slowing growth and a tough market are hurting Anthropic's valuation ahead of its planned November IPO.
Anthropic shared its quarterly numbers with potential investors at a private meeting in San Francisco, according to multiple US media reports.
Third-quarter revenue hit $16.8 billion.
That marks a roughly 45 percent jump from the second quarter and is more than 3.6 times the company's total annual revenue for 2025.
Growth has slowed, though.
In the second quarter, surging demand for the developer tool Claude Code had pushed revenue up by more than 140 percent compared to Q1.
Anthropic is far from that pace now, though a summer slowdown is one likely factor since people typically work less during those months and burn through fewer tokens.
OpenAI also launched a strong competitor with Astra in September, which Anthropic only successfully countered in late September with Opus 5.5.
The Financial Times reports this was the second straight quarter of adjusted profitability for the AI lab.
The company is cash-flow positive, too.
During the third quarter, Anthropic generated $1.70 in revenue for every dollar it spent on compute.
Anthropic also estimates that 5 to 7 percent of its revenue comes from distillation.

The two L-39 Albatros trainers Estonia uses are leased, according to the Estonian military’s website.
Their civilian status and lease terms would complicate any move to arm them, the former head of Estonia’s air force said back in April.
The proposal responds to a threat that is growing fast.
Yuriy Ihnat, a Ukrainian air force spokesman, said Ukraine intercepted about 40% of jet-powered drones in July and 60% in August, according to Hromadske.
In the same period, the number of jet-powered drones fired at Ukraine increased from a few hundred to several thousands a month.
Ukraine’s defense ministry puts their speed at more than 400 kilometers per hour.

Agility Robotics Inc. today said it is working with Nyobolt on a fast-recharge battery system for its Digit 5 system.

“For our customers, Digit’s uptime is the business case,” stated Daniel Diez, chief business officer at Agility.
“Digit 5 will deliver more than 20 hours of productive work in a 24-hour day, more than two full shifts.
That’s the kind of gain that materially improves the value customers get from Digit and the economics of deploying a humanoid robot fleet.

Nyobolt’s ultra-fast charging technology gets us there, and it’s one of the pieces that makes Digit 5 ready for full-scale operation.” Founded in 2015, Agility said Digit is “the first multi-purpose, human-centric robot that is ‘Made for Work’ and commercially deployed today.” The Salem, Ore.-based company said it has accumulated more than 65,000 of real-world operations .
Last month, it released Digit 5 with new legs and acknowledged that it is considering wheeled locomotion.

In May 2026, the company achieved a $1 billion valuation by raising $60 million including support from Symbotic Inc. “Nyobolt’s technology was chosen because Digit 5 will need more power from a smaller, lighter pack in environments where reliability isn’t optional,” said Sai Shivareddy, co-founder and CEO of Nyobolt.

“Agility set an exceptionally high bar for what a battery has to withstand in live warehouse and manufacturing environments, and this partnership shows what’s possible when ultra-fast charging is engineered for the toughest conditions in physical AI.” Digit 5 features longer runtime for humanoid customers Agility described Digit 5 as its first humanoid robot designed to work in close proximity to people safely and at scale.
The company asserted that this will let Digit 5 customers target longer operating windows, more productive shifts, and more demanding task sequences.

items.summary: Now, Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle is attempting to do something about it. Telle announced Monday at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting the creation of an enterprise-level Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning Task Force focused on soldiers’ quality of life. evidenceRecords.text: Now, Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle is attempting to do something about it.

Telle announced Monday at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting the creation of an enterprise-level Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning Task Force focused on soldiers’ quality of life.
The task force includes leaders from facility operations, contracting and military engineering who can “cut through bureaucratic silos,” the Army said in a Monday statement .
The announcement follows a directive from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last year to create another military-wide task force to improve barracks .
“Secretary of War Hegseth has said every service member deserves clean, comfortable, and safe housing,” Telle said at the annual meeting in Washington, D.C.

“This has never been done before — we’re taking this for the first time to the national level, to deliver results across the country to soldiers.” Jordan Gillis, assistant secretary of the Army for installations, energy and environment, said in a statement that HVAC is the top quality-of-life complaint that leadership hears from soldiers.

The Government Accountability Office reported in August that the Defense Department does not request enough funding to fully meet its installation maintenance and major improvement needs, leading to a backlog of deferred maintenance at barracks.
Hundreds of thousands of service members live in military barracks, with concerns about poor living conditions and management going back decades, according to the government watchdog.
Before the end of the fiscal year in September, the Army directed $15 million toward 44 high-priority HVAC projects across multiple installations, the service said in a statement.

“While that effort brought immediate relief to specific facilities, the [task force] leaders recognized that one-time emergency funding cannot replace a comprehensive, proactive strategy,” the Army said.
Members of the task force will work directly with garrison commanders to find HVAC projects for 2027 and 2028, the Army said.

items.title: Trump admin's retreat from foreign-influence fight is weakening US defenses, sources say
items.originalTitle: Trump admin's retreat from foreign-influence fight is weakening US defenses, sources say
items.summary: The Trump administration’s retreat from programs that track foreign influence operations has weakened various cross-sector relationships used to identify and confront those campaigns as midterm elections fast approach — even as artificial intelligence makes those operations easier to deploy — multiple sources told Nextgov/FCW . State officials say they are receiving fewer election-specific federal briefings than in previous cycles, while others who track foreign influence have observed routine exchanges with government and technology companies fall away.

evidenceRecords.text: The Trump administration’s retreat from programs that track foreign influence operations has weakened various cross-sector relationships used to identify and confront those campaigns as midterm elections fast approach — even as artificial intelligence makes those operations easier to deploy — multiple sources told Nextgov/FCW .

State officials say they are receiving fewer election-specific federal briefings than in previous cycles, while others who track foreign influence have observed routine exchanges with government and technology companies fall away.
Some also note that federal workforce departures have weakened cooperation with outside partners, including social media platforms, to track false information online.

While the federal government continues to gather intelligence on foreign threats to U.S. elections, some of those who lean on those findings say federal agencies are less reliably sharing information with non-federal researchers and state officials responsible for countering those campaigns.
That cooperation began to weaken before President Donald Trump returned to office, and his administration has since dismantled several programs dedicated to countering the problem.
This story is based on interviews with current and former federal officials, state election officials and specialists in cybersecurity and influence operations.

Their concerns come as fast-evolving AI tools now allow foreign influence operators to do more than just generate fake images or audio, instead helping them produce plausible-sounding messages, find audiences to target and autonomously adjust campaigns at a scale not seen before.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency referred questions about foreign malign influence to the Justice Department, saying that influence operations fall outside CISA’s mission.
“Election security is national security, and protecting our critical infrastructure remains a top priority for the Trump Administration, DHS, and CISA,” a CISA spokesperson said.
Foreign influence operations aim to shape what people believe and how they act, often without revealing who is behind the message.

items.originalTitle: Argonne Researchers Couple Spin Waves With Superconducting Circuits
items.summary: Insider Brief Researchers from Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign demonstrated a hybrid system that couples magnetic spin waves with superconducting circuits for quantum information processing. The experiment showed that information carried by spin waves in a thin magnetic film can transfer into microwave signals in a superconducting circuit, with the hybrid mode supporting one-way propagation.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Researchers from Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign demonstrated a hybrid system that couples magnetic spin waves with superconducting circuits for quantum information processing.

The experiment showed that information carried by spin waves in a thin magnetic film can transfer into microwave signals in a superconducting circuit, with the hybrid mode supporting one-way propagation.
The approach could support compact, on-chip quantum systems by combining spin-wave devices with superconducting circuit technology to help control signal direction and reduce unwanted feedback.
PRESS RELEASE — Quantum information systems could one day shape everyday life through faster computing and more secure communication.

A new result from the U.S. Department of Energy’s Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign marks an important step for magnetic spins — a quantum property of matter that can be used to store and manipulate information — to play a role in the future of quantum information processing.
The researchers show that the ripples in the magnetic state of a material, called spin waves, can interact with superconducting circuits, tiny circuits that can carry microwave signals.
The result is a hybrid system in which these two different ways of carrying information can work together.
Superconducting circuits, standard parts of many quantum information systems, help connect and control signals inside those systems.
They send and receive microwave signals in a way that strengthens communication with other parts of the device.
Spin waves offer a different advantage.
Under certain conditions, spin waves are unidirectional, meaning they naturally prefer one direction of travel over the opposite.
That is useful because quantum systems often need one-way signal control to help prevent unwanted noise from leaking back into the quantum components.

evidenceRecords.text: Israel’s relationships across Africa are shaped by competing priorities.

While the Gaza war has intensified diplomatic pressure and public opposition in many countries, security needs, commercial interests and longstanding bilateral partnerships continue to influence government decisions.
Since the war began in October 2023, South Africa has emerged as one of Israel’s most vocal critics in Africa.
Its government brought a case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), alleging violations of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
Israel rejects the allegations.
The court’s so-called provisional measures in 2024, including an order for Israel to take action to prevent acts of genocide, are not a final ruling on whether genocide has occurred.
In November 2023, South Africa’s National Assembly adopted a motion calling on the government to close the Israeli embassy and suspend diplomatic relations.
The motion did not itself implement those measures, but it underscored the strength of political opposition to Israel’s military campaign.
Some analysts have interpreted Israel’s renewed engagement with Zambia as an attempt to cultivate partners who could counterbalance South Africa’s influence in the region.
That remains an interpretation, not an established explanation for the relationship.

Zambia has its own reasons for seeking investment and cooperation, particularly in agriculture, water management and technology; closer bilateral ties alone do not prove that countering South Africa is Israel’s objective.
Professor Iwebunor Okwechime, of Obafemi Awolowo University, points to the historical roots of South Africa’s position towards Israel.
“If we trace the stance South Africa took, it goes back to the apartheid era, when Israel backed the apartheid regime and refused to support the struggle against the minority government.
This historical context is important for understanding South Africa-Israel relations today,” Okwechime told Al Jazeera.
For Israel, the upcoming election will test whether a new government can ease diplomatic tensions across Africa without fundamentally changing the policies that have fuelled them.

Thursday, Oct. 29 During U.S. spacewalk 100, NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk will exit the station’s Quest airlock to install and deploy an International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (IROSA) on the 2A electrical power channel.
The solar array will be the seventh IROSA and will provide additional power to support critical station operations, including its safe and controlled deorbit.
Thursday, Nov. 5 During U.S. spacewalk 101, Menon and Kutryk will install and deploy the eighth and final IROSA on the 3B channel of the space station, completing the power augmentation upgrades.
The final two roll-out solar arrays will complete the space station’s power system augmentation.
Together, the eight roll-out arrays will increase available power by up to 30%, boosting the station’s electric power generation capacity from 160 kilowatts to approximately 215 kilowatts.
NASA will share additional coverage details about U.S. spacewalks 100 and 101 closer to each operation on the agency’s live events web page and the space station blog .
The spacewalks will be the 285th and 286th conducted in support of space station assembly, maintenance, and upgrades.

Contractors and trucks are not being allowed to cross into Gaza and begin the work. “Israel won’t open the border,” they said.
A Board of Peace spokesperson declined to comment.
The Israeli Defense Forces and the Israeli government declined to comment.
Israel’s war in Gaza is one of the eight wars Trump claims to have resolved.
He listed it again last week in a screed on social media, protesting that it was unfair he had not won the Nobel peace prize.
The Board of Peace, formed in the wake of an October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza, is central to Trump’s claims to have ended the conflict.

Arkel’s planned “mission support site temporary outpost” is decidedly rudimentary: a fortified position of about 100 meters by 100 meters, at a site that was once part of the controversial and now defunct Gaza Humanitarian Foundation project, according to the person familiar with the matter.
The US-backed GHF operated in Gaza from May 2025 till October 2025 to deliver aid protected by private contractors.
The base would host short rotating deployments of a well-armed force of 150 troops in Gaza, the person said.
Israel’s refusal to allow Arkel, the contractor, to build the base, essentially cuts the Board of Peace off at the legs.

Representatives of Canada, Croatia, Egypt, Japan, Kuwait, Morocco, Albania and Panama signed a statement of intent to join the Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Marketplace during a ceremony Tuesday at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C. Robert Brown, president and CEO of AUSA, said that the signing brought the total number of participating nations to 33.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army’s online marketplace for rapid drone acquisition is expanding internationally.

Representatives of Canada, Croatia, Egypt, Japan, Kuwait, Morocco, Albania and Panama signed a statement of intent to join the Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Marketplace during a ceremony Tuesday at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C.
Robert Brown, president and CEO of AUSA, said that the signing brought the total number of participating nations to 33.
The marketplace was launched in March 2026 with nine European signers and continues to grow across regional allies and partners.
“With today’s signing, the marketplace is now truly a global effort,” said Brent Ingraham, assistant secretary of the Army for acquisition, logistics and technology.
More recently, the Army awarded counter-UAS contract vehicles worth $7 billion through the marketplace, Ingraham said.
The Army also operates a C-UAS Marketplace developed and operated by the Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF 401) for digital procurement of counter-drone systems.

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle, who attended the signing ceremony, said the drone marketplace was “connecting soldiers directly with builders and removing the bureaucratic middlemen.” Telle’s comments follow a Monday address to AUSA where he touted Army efforts to streamline acquisition.
The acting secretary further emphasized that the global drone marketplace builds on the Army’s demand for open architecture systems.

Telle said the Army needs to elevate open architectures beyond the tactical systems to “the strategic level,” saying the drone marketplace is a “great step forward” in sharing tactics, techniques, procedures and equipment with partners.

evidenceRecords.text: Amazon-owned Bee has launched its first new AI devices since its acquisition, including an updated wearable and a credit-card-sized recorder that attaches to smartphones.
The devices can summarize conversations, create to-do lists, and integrate with Alexa and Amazon shopping, with prices starting at $74.99.
Amazon’s personal AI wearable maker, Bee, is announcing its first new products since being acquired by the retail giant last year.

The tech company on Thursday introduced the Bee Frontier, the next generation of its device that can be worn on the wrist or pinned to clothes, along with Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of your smartphone.

The latter puts Bee into more direct competition with AI devices like the Plaud Note or Pocket, but at a lower price point — the Bee Frontier is $74.99, compared with $159 for the Plaud Note (or $189 for the Note Pro), or $129 for the Pocket AI device.

Like the original Bee, the idea with the new devices is to leverage AI to take notes from your everyday conversations, allowing you to remember the important things that were said, and then turn those into actionable to-dos, summaries, and insights.
All Bee devices can create conversation summaries and recaps for free, and offer 14 days of memory.
With an $11.99 per month Bee Pro subscription, users receive unlimited conversation summaries and integrations with Amazon.com, Alexa+, and third-party applications.
Pro users also get suggested to-dos, daily memories, a personal chat assistant, and conversation templates.
To make all this possible, Bee devices use a private computing security architecture, which doesn’t store the raw audio from your conversations.
Instead, audio is processed in real time and then deleted.

Transcripts of the conversation are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls, which means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you manually and intentionally share them.
In addition, you can opt to connect the Bee to Alexa, allowing your Echo device to use its ability to identify your voice, a feature called Voice ID, to recognize when you’re speaking.
It can then record your conversations to provide Bee’s insights. (This aspect of Bee is optional, and Amazon notes you can delete transcripts and summaries at any time.)
With its new connections to Amazon.com and Alexa, Bee users can make purchases from Amazon or ask Alexa for their Bee insights, summaries, or to-dos hands-free.
