items.title: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
items.originalTitle: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
items.summary: Starlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on. For Ukraine, it is vital for communications on the battlefield and effective drone warfare. But on Tuesday night, Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield "missions", a top Ukrainian official said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks.

evidenceRecords.text: It is the "backbone of military communications in Ukraine" that provides vital high-speed internet to forces across the country.
Starlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on.
For Ukraine, it is vital for communications on the battlefield and effective drone warfare.
But on Tuesday night, Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection.
This disrupted some battlefield "missions", a top Ukrainian official said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks.

"Starlink gives Ukraine the ability to see what's coming, to protect people," Kurt Volker, former US ambassador to Nato, told the BBC's Radio 4 Today programme. "If you cut that off, then more people are going to get killed - and that is a very cynical and callous decision to slow that down the way that has been done."
The move has once again shown how Starlink can impact the conflict, which has been raging since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Starlink is an internet network that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and battlefields.
The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia.
Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February, giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict.

Put simply, Starlink uses its thousands of satellites to ping high-speed internet back to almost every corner of the globe, using terminals on the ground that users can easily buy and set up themselves.
As Musk said, they have two instructions: "point at sky, plug in".
In Ukraine, both Starlink (the civilian service) and Starshield (the military service) are used, depending on what communications are needed.
"Starlink gives Ukraine the ability to see what's coming, to protect people," Kurt Volker, former US ambassador to Nato, told the BBC's Radio 4 Today programme.
Because Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, when Ukraine sends long-range missiles deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

items.originalTitle: FirstQFM Model Cuts Single-Qubit Gate Times by 33% on QuantWare Processor
items.summary: Insider Brief FirstQFM applied its quantum foundation model to a 21-qubit QuantWare superconducting processor at the Israeli Quantum Computing Center, reducing single-qubit gate execution time by 33% without reducing gate fidelity. The model generated custom pulse-level gate implementations from existing calibration data and identified five qubit pairs with improved Bell-state fidelity, with the improvements confirmed in independent hardware runs.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief FirstQFM applied its quantum foundation model to a 21-qubit QuantWare superconducting processor at the Israeli Quantum Computing Center, reducing single-qubit gate execution time by 33% without reducing gate fidelity.

The model generated custom pulse-level gate implementations from existing calibration data and identified five qubit pairs with improved Bell-state fidelity, with the improvements confirmed in independent hardware runs.

The work used Quantum Machines’ control and calibration infrastructure alongside NVIDIA accelerated computing, and FirstQFM plans to expand its optimizations as QuantWare develops larger quantum processors.
PRESS RELEASE — FirstQFM today announced results from applying FirstQFM’s quantum foundation model to a QuantWare superconducting quantum processor at the Israeli Quantum Computing Center (IQCC).
FirstQFM ’s foundation model builds on top of Quantum Machines’ native calibration stack, and generated single-qubit gates that reduced execution time by 33% on a QuantWare Contralto-D21 QPU.
Gates were validated directly on the QuantWare processor using randomized benchmarking with no loss of gate fidelity.
The model generated custom pulse-level implementations of gates from calibration data produced by the Quantum Machines’ calibration stack with no additional quantum hardware measurements required.
This shifts more of the gate optimization process from scarce QPU time to classical compute.
The model also identified improvements to two-qubit gates, which are central to entanglement and typically more challenging to calibrate than single-qubit operations.

Using existing calibration data together with a short hardware probe, the model identified five qubit pairs with higher Bell-state fidelity with each improvement confirmed in independent hardware runs.

FirstQFM developed its foundation model using NVIDIA accelerated computing hardware and software, including the Leonardo supercomputer and the NVIDIA CUDA-Q open source hybrid platform, before fine-tuning and applying the model to the QuantWare processor.

“On QuantWare ’s processor, our model was able to use existing calibration data to generate shorter single-qubit gates while preserving fidelity, and to improve selected two-qubit operations.” As superconducting quantum processors grow, calibration becomes a harder control problem.

New materials have traditionally been invented using trial-and-error experiments (a slow process) or randomly generating candidates on a computer and screening the results (which is computationally expensive).

A game changer is inverse design—a target property is specified initially (e.g., the specific band gap or formation energy), and AI rapidly and directly designs a matching structure for a stable crystal.
Generative machine learning models, which learn from existing crystal data, are well suited to this task because they can create entirely new materials.

The chemical and physical properties of a crystalline material (e.g., the hardness, electrical conductivity and optical behavior) depend on atomic-scale properties: the crystal structure (the arrangement of molecules in a repeating three-dimensional pattern) and the electronic structure (how electrons are distributed among energy levels and around atoms).
For target values of the formation energy and band gap, MatterGen-e⁻ produced substantially more structures that were simultaneously valid, stable, unique and novel than MatterGen.

By outputting electronic descriptors together with each structure, MatterGen-e⁻ also provides the density of states of newly generated materials, which agreed reasonably well with first-principles calculations.

These findings point to a design principle for generative models in materials science: using physically meaningful intermediate representations, such as electronic structure, rather than atomic structure alone.
Using electronic structure to guide AI in designing new materials (2026, October 15)

According to the company, the new vehicle, also called the “Kaaiman,” was derived from the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle , or JLTV, and adapted for the Netherlands Ministry of Defence .

At the 2026 AUSA Annual Meeting and Exposition, Pat Williams, the company’s chief program officer, described the “production” as “an important step in delivering next-generation capability to the Netherlands.” Compared to a standard JLTV, the DXPV has been enhanced for mobility, corrosion protection, mission systems and suspension for increased off-road performance.

“Just as importantly, it demonstrates the strength of an active production base and our ability to continuously evolve proven vehicle technologies to address the changing needs of our customers and their missions,” Williams said.

Beyond the DXPV prototype, Oshkosh officials at the show are emphasizing the company’s renewed approach toward “rapidly delivering mission-ready solutions.” The company added that it has delivered more than 200,000 tactical wheeled vehicles to U.S. and allied forces.
The Oshkosh AUSA booth also featured other platforms like its Family of Medium Tactical Vehicle A2 Low-Velocity Air Drop, or FMTV A2 LVAD, and the hybrid electric JLTV, or simply eJLTV.
With that, Williams added that “production readiness matters,” referring to how quickly Oshkosh was able to develop the DXPV.
The Dutch MoD signed an agreement with Oshkosh for the vehicles last summer and then placed an order valued between $25 and $30 million in January.
“Because we’re building on a mature platform from an active production line, we can move from concept to prototype much faster than traditional vehicle development,” Williams said.

“It’s really important to predict both, but extreme events might be the most impactful part of this for society.” Joining Cohen on the paper are lead authors Hannah Guan, a Harvard College undergraduate; Soukayna Mouatadid, a University of Toronto postdoc; Genevieve Flaspohler SM ’18, PhD ’22; Paulo Orenstein, an associate professor at Brazil’s National Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics; Jeremy Berman of the data company DTN; Jakob Schloer and Joshua Talib, researchers with the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts; and Alex Lu, Haiyu Dong, Jonathan Weyn, Zekun Ni, and

Longer forecasts In the 1970s, longtime MIT Professor Edward Lorenz came up with the idea of chaos theory to describe how tiny changes in initial weather conditions lead to completely different outcomes.

“He came up with this theoretical two-week limit where beyond that, we just can’t predict weather because the noise in the system grows so much that it overwhelms any signal you start with,” Cohen says.

items.summary: Of these, thermal management has emerged as one of the most critical areas for successfully deploying co-packaged optics (CPO) in hyperscale AI environments. Ayar Labs and Global Unichip Corp. (GUC) jointly conducted thermal co-simulation of the advanced package design and determined the thermal floor map for the package and subsequent chiplets, including air- and liquid-cooled environments. evidenceRecords.text: Of these, thermal management has emerged as one of the most critical areas for successfully deploying co-packaged optics (CPO) in hyperscale AI environments.

Ayar Labs and Global Unichip Corp. (GUC) jointly conducted thermal co-simulation of the advanced package design and determined the thermal floor map for the package and subsequent chiplets, including air- and liquid-cooled environments.
Our co-simulation data show that CPO can operate reliably within the thermal envelope of advanced multi-chip packages.
Novel design enables over 100 Tbps speeds Let’s start with the new multi-chip package (MCP) design that integrates Ayar Labs’ TeraPHY optical engines into GUC’s advanced packaging and ASIC workflow.
The new XPU MCP design replaces traditional electrical interconnects with Ayar Labs’ optical engines, which are attached directly to the MCP organic substrate.
What is thermal co-simulation and why is it important?
Thermal co-simulation is the combined simulation of electrical behavior and heat flow across a chip.

In GUC’s thermal integrity design flow, we consider every chip’s power maps and perform thermal crosstalk and dynamic thermal co-simulation to ensure the MCP’s thermal integrity from early-stage through sign-off.
Thermal co-simulation is crucial for GUC’s advanced ASIC workflows.

evidenceRecords.text: The G20 finance ministers and central bank governors are gathering in Bangkok, Thailand, on Thursday amid an uncertain global outlook shaped by the US-Israel war on Iran.
The meetings are being held in conjunction with the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, taking place in the Thai capital from October 12 to October 18.

The G20 is an economic forum comprising 19 large economies, including the United States, China, the United Kingdom, Australia, Brazil, India, Japan, Indonesia and Saudi Arabia, as well as the European Union and the African Union.
Together, the G20 countries account for about 85 percent of global gross domestic product (GDP) and three-quarters of global trade.

The G20 was established in 1999 as a forum for finance ministers and central bank governors to address shared economic concerns in the wake of the Asian Financial Crisis, before expanding into a broader forum for national leaders.
Most finance ministers and central bank governors of the G20 will be in Bangkok, along with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva and World Bank Group President Ajay Banga.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will be a notable absence from the gatherings, as the top economic official of the world’s biggest economy and G20 chair.
The G20 meeting, one of several gatherings of the group’s finance ministers each year, will help shape the agenda for the headline leaders’ summit in Miami, Florida, taking place on December 14-15.
G20 members will also bring more specific individual concerns to the table based on their economic and geopolitical priorities.

At the last meeting of G20 finance ministers in Asheville, North Carolina, US, held on August 31 and September 1, member countries failed to issue a joint communique after China objected to language to do with trade.

This year, a drought accompanying El Niño has left the Amazon rainforest primed to burn, and scientists say the region has entered the early stages of what they think will be a long and severe fire season.

Starting in September 2026, satellites detected sharp increases in fire activity and smoke emissions in the central and eastern Amazon, visible in fire and emissions monitoring platforms including NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED), and NASA Worldview .

When the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Aqua satellite captured this image of smoke streaming from fires on both sides of the Amazon River on October 12, 2026, heavy smoke socked in Manaus, the capital of the Brazilian state of Amazonas.
The pattern begins along the equator with drought and peat fires in Indonesia , followed by elevated fire activity in this part of the Amazon.
“Now, in the Amazon, we’re seeing the second domino in the cascade fall,” Morton said, referring to the uptick in fires that has begun in Pará and Amazonas.
It’s so wet in the Brazilian Amazon that lightning ignites less than 1 percent of fires, so the vast majority of fires currently burning there were started by people, Morton said.

The large fires in this region began as management fires—clearing shrubs from pastures or crops from fields, for instance—but have escaped and are now burning freely through the parched understory of the rainforest, he added.

He plans to share the locations of these “candidate fires” with scientists at MapBiomas , a multi-institutional network comprising universities, NGOs, and technology companies that maps fires and land-use change in the Amazon.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief EigenOrbit has released eigenkit 1.0, a free, open-source Python library designed to run quantum algorithms across multiple simulators and quantum hardware platforms without rewriting the algorithm for each backend.

The library supports tools including Qiskit, PennyLane, NVIDIA CUDA-Q and Amazon Braket, alongside hardware from IBM and IQM, and includes algorithms for quantum machine learning, optimization, chemistry and finance.

Released under the Apache 2.0 license, eigenkit includes quantum-versus-classical benchmarking and cost warnings before paid hardware jobs, with packages available through PyPI and source code on GitHub.
PRESS RELEASE — EigenOrbit has released eigenkit, a free open-source Python library for quantum computing.
With eigenkit, a quantum algorithm is written once and runs on a simulator on an ordinary laptop or on real quantum computers from IBM, IQM and the vendors available through Amazon Braket.
Quantum teams today often pick a simulator or a hardware vendor first and then write code against that vendor’s SDK.
EigenOrbit uses eigenkit as the foundation of its own platform for comparing quantum and classical approaches on industrial problems.

EigenOrbit has released eigenkit 1.0, a free, open-source Python library designed to run quantum algorithms across multiple simulators and quantum hardware platforms without rewriting the algorithm for each backend.
Moving from one machine to another takes a single setting, and the rest of the code stays as it was.
Yet no single backend suits every workload.

Quantum processors differ in qubit count, connectivity, native gates, error rates, price and queue times, so the best device can change from one circuit to the next. eigenkit separates the definition of an algorithm from the machine that executes it, which makes trying several backends a routine step.
Many machines, one codebase. eigenkit runs on its own built-in simulator and on PennyLane, Qiskit, Qiskit Aer, Qulacs, qsim, TensorCircuit, NVIDIA CUDA-Q and Amazon Braket simulators.
On hardware it supports IBM quantum computers, IQM quantum computers and the processors available on Amazon Braket.
Photonic circuits run through Quandela’s Perceval.
Familiar tools. eigenkit works with PyTorch and scikit-learn, the libraries most data scientists already use.
The library comes from a team that has built quantum software for industrial clients in finance, energy, healthcare and manufacturing for more than five years.

items.summary: If you’ve ever had your car start sluggishly, or not at all, on a particularly frigid winter morning, you know standard batteries do not like extreme cold. That’s why NASA researchers are working to develop a battery that could function in the brutal cold of the Moon’s South Pole, where nighttime temperatures plunge to minus 328 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 200 Celsius).

evidenceRecords.text: The project is called Solid Power for Extreme Environment Adaptability and Resilience in Space (SPEARS), and it could provide NASA with an important tool to help power humanity’s sustained presence on the Moon through the Artemis campaign.

“We will need them on the Moon, too, and these batteries will be required to operate reliably and safely in this harsh environment.

NASA/Ryan Hill Splashy problem, solid solution Traditional lithium-ion batteries like those in your cell phone and laptop have a critical weakness: they rely on liquid electrolytes.

NASA/Ryan Hill Power for Moon, Earth The applications for these solid-state batteries are nearly limitless, from small tools like drills that must operate in shadowed lunar craters, to rovers and emergency power packs for astronauts.
If you’ve ever had your car start sluggishly, or not at all, on a particularly frigid winter morning, you know standard batteries do not like extreme cold.

That’s why NASA researchers are working to develop a battery that could function in the brutal cold of the Moon’s South Pole, where nighttime temperatures plunge to minus 328 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 200 Celsius).

For future lunar operations, a battery will need to work immediately when warmed up and be able to power everything from an astronaut’s emergency kit to a rover capable of exploring the Moon’s darkest craters — all without posing a fire hazard.
A team of NASA researchers is working to make all that happen.

“Batteries have become an important part of our lives here on Earth, which enable our laptops, cell phones, power tools, and even our vehicles,” said Donald Dornbusch, principal investigator for SPEARS at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, where the project is led. “We will need them on the Moon, too, and these batteries will be required to operate reliably and safely in this harsh environment.
That’s why we’re working on this technology.”
Traditional lithium-ion batteries like those in your cell phone and laptop have a critical weakness: they rely on liquid electrolytes.
Cool a conventional battery to the Moon’s nighttime temperatures, and that liquid would freeze, potentially damaging the battery.
Heat it up too much — say, to daytime lunar temperatures of 212 F (100 C) — and it won’t work until cooled.
Expose the liquid to the vacuum of space, and it evaporates.
SPEARS batteries solve these problems by replacing the liquid electrolyte with a solid ceramic- or polymer-based material.

items.title: Google says self-improving AI isn't anywhere close
items.originalTitle: Google says self-improving AI isn't anywhere close
items.summary: Google engineer Haydn Belfield says self-improving AI remains far off, even as significant automation is already taking hold. Google Deepmind has seen no measurable acceleration of AI research driven by AI itself, according to Belfield. That doesn't mean significant automation isn't happening already: AI now writes more than 75 percent of production code. But about 88 percent of code changes still need human oversight or review, and every change is reviewed by a human before submission, according to Belfield. The share of code changes fully delegated to AI rose from 7.5 to 11.9 percent.

evidenceRecords.text: A month after President Donald Trump intervened to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea, citing a desire not to upset his “very good relationship” with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un, the commander of Army forces on the peninsula said he’d like to go bigger – both in exercise frequency and geographic scope.

Xavier Brunson, commander of United Nations Command, Combined Forces Command, and United States Forces Korea, said lessons from Ukraine prompted interest in changing the shape and structure of exercises there.

“I think what we recognize is that largely the two big exercises every year in Korea focus on large command posts; we’ve got to move away from that,” Brunson said, in response to a question from a Korean journalist.

Speaking at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting here Monday, Gen. Xavier Brunson, commander of United Nations Command, Combined Forces Command, and United States Forces Korea, said lessons from Ukraine prompted interest in changing the shape and structure of exercises there.

“So, what we intend to do is take advantage of the knowledge that we have of the threats that exist or that prevail in the Ukraine fight,” he continued. “We’re trying to say how might we train differently, and so [Gen. Kim Sung-min, deputy commander of the Republic of Korea–U.S. Combined Forces Command] and I talk about how we would operate in a distributed fashion.”

In light of the distributed fight and scope of battle in Ukraine, Brunson suggested a training exercise that spanned from Jeju Island to Gyeonggi Province — a distance of nearly 300 miles across nearly the full span of the Korean peninsula.

“Just imagine if we trained across the entirety of the peninsula and got ourselves in a shape where we would say, ‘You can’t utilize the things that you’ve learned in the fight in the battlefield in Ukraine on us, because we learn the same lessons and we’ve distributed ourselves in such a way that we don’t make ourselves the target,” he said.

evidenceRecords.text: BBC Verify has identified 254 incidents in which the Israeli military has been accused of killing or injuring people in Gaza, Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Israel that it said it was investigating, but have no public outcome.

Using purpose-built AI tools, BBC Verify combed through more than 60,000 news reports and examined hundreds of incidents in which the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) faced allegations of harm since the start of the Gaza war.
Following extensive manual checking of each incident, we found 300 cases that the military said it was looking into, only 28 of which had outcomes published on the IDF website.
For a further 18 incidents it was unclear if the investigation has been concluded.

BBC Verify approached the IDF about each case multiple times but only received information on two incidents, which the IDF said are still under review. "The IDF takes every allegation or report raising concerns about conduct that may be inconsistent with the law or IDF directives with the utmost seriousness," it said in a statement.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which works in warzones to uphold the Geneva Conventions, publishes guidelines that state investigations into potential violations of international humanitarian law, whether criminal or otherwise, should be as transparent as possible.
Despite multiple requests, the IDF has not provided a transparent breakdown of the status of the 300 investigations identified by BBC Verify.

Dan Owen, a researcher at Yesh Din which has been monitoring military investigations since 2006, told BBC Verify that he believes the IDF will often try to "prolong" investigations. "They try to stretch out these processes to the point where people forget and people don't care about them," he said.
More than 1,000 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces since 11 October 2023, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, external.

items.title: AI drone outpaces former world champions using one camera and no GPS
items.originalTitle: AI drone outpaces former world champions using one camera and no GPS
items.summary: What does it take for an autonomous robot to be faster around a course than human drone pilots? At these dizzying speeds, humans need lightning-fast reflexes. Researchers at Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have developed an AI system that enables a racing drone to navigate demanding courses at extreme speed using only a single camera. It outperformed even former world champion human drone pilots in a race.

evidenceRecords.text: Researchers at Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have developed an AI system that enables a racing drone to navigate demanding courses at extreme speed using only a single camera.
It outperformed even former world champion human drone pilots in a race.
What does it take for an autonomous robot to be faster around a course than human drone pilots?
At these dizzying speeds, humans need lightning-fast reflexes.

Now published in Science Robotics, the scientific work behind this accomplishment shows how compact, efficient neural-network-based control can achieve high-performance autonomous flight under real-world conditions.
The underlying principles could help advance a much broader class of autonomous robots, from vehicles to mobile and humanoid systems.
The TU Delft team set out to investigate how far artificial intelligence can push a drone with very limited sensors, onboard computing power and energy.
This is a challenging problem: at high speed, even a small delay in sensing or control can mean missing a gate, colliding with an obstacle or losing control and crashing.
At high speed, the drone has very little time to interpret what it sees.
A neural network identifies the racing gates in the camera images, while the onboard IMU and a model of the drone estimate its position and motion.
The system does all this without GPS or external motion tracking.

"We developed a robust way of combining what the camera sees with the drone's own motion information, allowing it to navigate the track at high speed without GPS." The system also had to cope with imperfections that occur in real flight, including camera interference and sensor saturation.
For Guido de Croon, professor at Delft University of Technology, the value of drone racing goes beyond making drones fly faster.
In the current study, we made an AI efficient enough to control a drone traveling at 100 kilometers per hour (62 miles per hour) using a single camera and a small onboard processor.

items.title: NASA’s Chandra Breaks Down ‘Treble Clef’s’ Galaxy Cluster Collision
items.originalTitle: NASA’s Chandra Breaks Down ‘Treble Clef’s’ Galaxy Cluster Collision
items.summary: Wolk Astronomers have used NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the “Treble Clef” because its distinct shape strongly resembles the musical symbol. The researchers discovered the Treble Clef is likely caused by an outburst from a supermassive black hole, followed by a collision of two galaxy clusters.

evidenceRecords.text: Wolk Astronomers have used NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the “Treble Clef” because its distinct shape strongly resembles the musical symbol.
The researchers discovered the Treble Clef is likely caused by an outburst from a supermassive black hole, followed by a collision of two galaxy clusters.

An explanation for the Treble Clef has been particularly difficult to find because the formation lies almost directly behind the plane of the Milky Way, meaning that stars, gas, and dust from our home galaxy largely block the view from Earth.

NASA’s Chandra and the German Extended RÖntgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array (eROSITA) X-ray telescope found diffuse, hot gas at the location of the Treble Clef, showing that a galaxy cluster hosts the object.
The researchers also determined the galaxy cluster is, in fact, two clusters in the process of merging.
Galaxy clusters are some of the largest structures in the universe, containing hundreds of individual galaxies and huge reservoirs of superheated gas.

This new composite image of the Treble Clef and its cluster shows the multimillion-degree gas detected in X-rays by Chandra and eROSITA in blue, with some of the Chandra data derived from a special technique the authors used to highlight important features in the Chandra data.
Radio data shown in red from the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR), a large network of radio telescopes in Europe reveals the doppelganger of the musical notation.
The final piece of the combined image comes from infrared data obtained by the United Kingdom Infrared Telescope, appearing mostly white.
The authors concluded that the Treble Clef likely formed in a two-stage process.
First, an earlier outburst from a supermassive black hole in the galaxy cluster’s center drove clouds of charged particles and magnetic fields away at close to the speed of light.
This led to a type of cosmic crescendo and initially produced bright radio waves that later faded as the particles lost energy.

items.originalTitle: How to earn the US Army’s Jungle tab in Panama — and lose 10lbs
items.summary: BASE AERONAVAL CRISTÓBAL COLÓN, Panama — Though many service members venture into the hot, humid terrain of the U.S. Army’s jungle school in Panama , not all leave with the newly authorized-for-wear Jungle tab. evidenceRecords.text: BASE AERONAVAL CRISTÓBAL COLÓN, Panama — Though many service members venture into the hot, humid terrain of the U.S. Army’s jungle school in Panama , not all leave with the newly authorized-for-wear Jungle tab.
The Panama course, back after a decades-long hiatus, resumed in 2025 as the U.S. military shifted its focus to the Western Hemisphere.
In August, the Army confirmed it had approved the small arch-shaped patch — emblazoned with the word “Jungle” — for service-wide wear on the left shoulder.

Those who attended the course from 1990 to 1999 at Fort Sherman, now known as Base Aeronaval Cristóbal Colón, are authorized the tab retroactively , as well as those who attended the 12-day jungle school in Oahu, Hawaii, after Fort Sherman’s closure.

The 18-day course includes classes on flora, fauna, machetes, jungle first aid, fire-starting, shelter-building, and more, but showing up and trudging through muddy terrain in crippling Panama humidity is not enough to earn the tab.
“There’s a difference between graduating the course with the tab and finishing the course,” said Lt.
Andrew Eagan, the officer in charge of the Jungle Operations Training Course in Panama, or JOTC-P.
Even if students fail one part of the curriculum, as long as their failure presents no medical or safety issues, they must finish the course.
There are then five critical tasks across the course that you have to pass in order to graduate with the tab,” Eagen said.
Combat Water Survival Assessment and 5K Early in the course, participants face physical fitness tests.

The Combat Water Survival Assessment, or CWSA, requires participants to complete a variety of survival tasks in the water, including swimming in combat gear, ditching their equipment and dropping from a meters-high diving board.
The 5-kilometer run — only 3.1 miles — has proven one of the course’s toughest obstacles for many jungle school candidates.

items.summary: The Australian counter-drone technology company has announced its Q4 2026 software release, introducing enhancements across detection, identification, tracking, and drone defeat. The update is available through its Mission Ready Services subscription, which provides ongoing software improvements to more than 4,200 software-enabled devices deployed in the field. evidenceRecords.text: The Australian counter-drone technology company has announced its Q4 2026 software release, introducing enhancements across detection, identification, tracking, and drone defeat.
The update is available through its Mission Ready Services subscription, which provides ongoing software improvements to more than 4,200 software-enabled devices deployed in the field.
One of the key changes helps operators spot unfamiliar drone signals before they appear in DroneShield’s existing threat library.

Its RfRecon system can now forward signals that resemble drone activity directly to the DroneSentry-C2 dashboard, allowing teams to investigate potential new threats sooner and filter records by frequency range.
The update also improves camera-based detection and classification.
DroneShield reports a 44% improvement in thermal camera classification accuracy, along with an 18% increase in precision and an 8% improvement in recall when identifying fixed-wing drones.
Target detection in standard video has also been improved.
Another enhancement connects radio frequency (RF) sensing with optical cameras for passive drone detection and tracking.
Operators can visually verify detected targets without using radar or transmitting emissions that could reveal their position.
With compatible Bosch Starlight cameras, teams can direct cameras toward the source of an RF detection before locking onto and tracking the drone.
The software also introduces coordinated response capabilities across connected DroneSentry-X Mk2 systems.
When one unit detects a threat, it can share that detection with other connected units, enabling them to coordinate disruption efforts.
“Drone threats change constantly, and counter-drone capability has to keep pace long after it is deployed,” says Angus Bean, DroneShield’s CEO.

items.originalTitle: Eye-inspired cameras help new system detect fast-moving drones in complex skies
items.summary: Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) has developed a new tool that uses neuromorphic cameras to detect unmanned aerial system (UAS) drones. SwRI's Hierax system pairs event-based cameras, dynamic sensing technology that mimics the power of human eyesight, with custom software to detect fast-moving drones in complex aerial scenarios. evidenceRecords.text: Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) has developed a new tool that uses neuromorphic cameras to detect unmanned aerial system (UAS) drones.
SwRI's Hierax system pairs event-based cameras, dynamic sensing technology that mimics the power of human eyesight, with custom software to detect fast-moving drones in complex aerial scenarios.

"Our approach potentially transforms any UAS into an autonomous precision interceptor designed to detect, track, pursue and neutralize rogue or hostile drones without manual piloting," said Kase Saylor, an SwRI research manager. "By leveraging neuromorphic sensing, we provide a hardware-agnostic intercept kit that bridges the gap between detection and neutralization."
The evolution of drone warfare in Ukraine has demonstrated a critical need for counter-UAS technologies to support the U.S. military and its allies.
Drones are commonly detected using radar, radio frequency signals, acoustics, thermal imaging or optical cameras.
Event-based, or neuromorphic, cameras offer advantages because they do not emit signals that can be jammed by adversaries while offering reduced size, weight, power and costs.

Neuromorphic cameras capture even slight changes in brightness at the pixel level, much like biological eyesight, unlike optical cameras that only capture individual frames of light in red, green and blue wavelengths.
Although event-based cameras have been a topic of interest in laboratory research for decades, they have only recently been adapted to operate in complex environments.
The SwRI solution requires less computing power than standard optical sensing systems that rely on complex machine learning.

"By keeping up with the latest research and applying it to real-world applications, we are committed to helping our clients leverage the latest advancements in technology, such as neuromorphic cameras," said David Anthony, an SwRI engineer who led the research.
SwRI used a modular open systems approach to develop the Hierax imaging package to meet U.S. Department of Defense requirements for battlefield interoperability across combined joint task forces.

This approach allows AI to create intricate patterns, including wave-like designs, which the pair said they plan to share more about in the future.

items.originalTitle: Characterization of HBM Power Consumption (ETH Zurich, NYU)
items.summary: Researchers at ETH Zürich and New York University published a technical paper titled “Understanding the Power Consumption of Modern High Bandwidth Memory: Experimental Analysis and Modeling Using Real HBM2 DRAM Chips.” Abstract Excerpt: “We perform the first comprehensive experimental characterization of power consumed by real HBM2 DRAM chips. Our extensive characterization yields 1) the empirical basis for developing new, accurate HBM power models or validating existing power models and 2) key insights into structural and data-pattern-dependent variation of power in HBM2 chips.

evidenceRecords.text: Researchers at ETH Zürich and New York University published a technical paper titled “Understanding the Power Consumption of Modern High Bandwidth Memory: Experimental Analysis and Modeling Using Real HBM2 DRAM Chips.” Abstract Excerpt: “We perform the first comprehensive experimental characterization of power consumed by real HBM2 DRAM chips.

Our extensive characterization yields 1) the empirical basis for developing new, accurate HBM power models or validating existing power models and 2) key insights into structural and data-pattern-dependent variation of power in HBM2 chips.

Out of our 13 new findings and 6 key takeaway messages, we highlight: 1) a read operation consumes significantly higher current than any other operation and 2) the toggled data bus signals in a data transfer burst significantly affect current draw where toggling all HBM2-internal bank group bus signals causes 29.4% higher power consumption than keeping them constant.

Leveraging our empirical insights into HBM2 power consumption, we engineer an access pattern that yields 23.6% higher power consumption on average across 36 tested HBM2 chips than the highest-power-consuming JEDEC-specified current measurement loop.” Find the technical paper here .
